newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Strong pound hits Comm Union profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strong pound hits Comm Union profits.

text.p: British insurance giant Commercial Union plans to continue expansion in life businesses despite reporting a decline in annual profits on Wednesday caused largely by strong sterling.
Commercial's operating pretax profit fell to 444 million pounds ($726.2 million) from 509 million, mainly on a 64 million pound loss caused by exchange rate changes.
The company offered a final dividend of 18.85 pence per share making a it a total 30.30 pence for the full year.
Commercial Union's net asset value slid to 545 pence, from 582 pence in 1995 and was below the average expectations of 570 to 572 pence.
Investors reacted to the asset value dip, and CU shares fell to 669-3/4 pence from Tuesday's 690 pence close before recovering to 676p before midsession.
"The results are at the bottom end of expectations," said an insurance analyst.
Commercial Union's finance director Peter Foster, however, said the situation was looking up for the group, as was reflected in its fourth quarter in 1996.
Commercial beat the strong pound in the last quarter with operating pretax profit of 123 million pounds, against 121 million in the corresponding period in the previous year.
Measured against similar rates of exchange, the 1995 fourth quarter stood at 105 million sterling.
In the entire 1996 the pound strengthened 10 percent against the dollar, 17 percent againt the French franc and around 12 percent against the mark.
The increases affected Commercial Union which has operations in 16 countries, making it more globally exposed than its other British competitors.
Foster said the group would continue to expand in its life insurance business and would be interested in acquisitions to stimulate further growth.
"Our strategy of more emphasis on life business has proved viable so far...we will be looking at any suitable acquisition that may come across," Foster said.
Life business accounts for 44 percent of Commercial's net written premiums.
The group's life business grew 25 percent -- at comparable rates of exchange -- to 2.9 billion pounds. Single premium sales wre 20 percent higher, helped by growth in the Netherlands, UK, and France.
Profits from general insurance fell 21 percent to 356 million pounds which included an increase of 41 million in weather claims in the United States.
Shareholders' funds amounted to 3.902 billion against 4.07 billion in the previous year but Commercial also made an equilisation provision of 70 million pounds.
Foster said the British insurance sector, which faced pressure of declining premiums during most of the last two years, is expected to look up in 1997 with hopes for higher rates.
"It (a resurgence) is inevitable. Though the results in the UK would remain down," Foster said.
He said Commercial Union's expense ratio has been "very good" in the UK and has given it an advantage vis-a-vis its competitors.
"Its been three percent better than others," he said.
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
